docs.text: It is an epically bad to allow cargo vessels entering Great Lakes to avoid ballast water treatment. 🌊🌊

The harms caused by invasive species spread through ballast water are catastrophic, well documented, and felt by the people who live and work around the Great Lakes. www.detroitnews.com/story/busine...

Vector management (regulation of ship ballast water release) has caused an unprecedented 85% decline in the rate of invasion of the Great Lakes. Canada & USA (2006-08) mandated open-ocean flushing of saltwater thru ships' ballast tanks - with success. conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10....

Protecting the Great Lakes means stopping invasive species at the source. We’re challenging a final rule from the U.S. EPA that lets most existing cargo vessels avoid modern ballast water treatment, allowing invasive species to spread between ports.

#InvasiveSpecies transported in ballast water are often tiny, but they can cause huge problems in the #GreatLakes. Learn how scientists, regulators, and the shipping industry work together to control this invasion pathway: #NISAW

Bureau of Reclamation launched a new three-phase prize challenge to identify innovative solutions that prevent the spread of aquatic invasive species through watercraft ballast compartments in the Great Lakes. www.usbr.gov/newsroom/new... #906Life #PureMichigan

Quote: "By the late 1990s, the states and provinces around the Great Lakes had agreed to require ships entering the Great Lakes to treat their ballast water. Since then, ballast-water invasions into the Great Lakes have nearly stopped. " Inaccurate. It was the 2006-08 reg that reduced bw invasions.

This goes beyond that, this is Great Lakes tankers that never need to leave the Great Lakes but they are moving all around the lakes and spreading the invasive species far and wide from port to port. They aren't being held to the same ballast rules for ships coming into the Seaway.
They were brought in by international ships that emptied their ballast water into the Great Lakes and introducing all kinds of invasive critters.
The tankers are the ones who have moved the mussels to every corner of our Great Lakes because they still have not fixed their ballast systems because of "costs".

They are looking for a solution to prevent Great Lakes tankers from moving mussels around the lakes from port to port. They are the reason we are in this mess.

The Michigan EGLE account on Twitter told me that ocean going freighters were sanitizing their ballast water before entering the St Lawrence seaway. I didn't believe them then and don't believe them now. Oceans ships have destroyed the Great Lakes with invasives.

Ballast water treatment has been tremendously effective in preventing new invasive species introductions in the Great Lakes. The shipping industry has kept a close eye on recent EPA plans to update ballast water regulations:
Stricter ballast rules on freighters demanded to protect Great Lakes from invasive species www.chicagotribune.com/2026/02/01/g...

The problem now isn't the rules and regulations for ballast cleaning systems for new ships. It is the old ships, which makes up the vast majority of the Great Lakes fleet that is doing massive ongoing damage moving mussels around from port to port. It is a loop hole and it is fueled by greed.

U.S. EPA regulations exempt existing Great Lakes-only ships ("lakers") from installing new ballast water treatment systems. While new, newly built vessels are required to have treatment, the current, older fleet is exempt due to high retrofit costs and operational challenges.

Even before Donald Trump took office for a second term, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finalized a rule that weakened ballast water discharge requirements for large vessels on the Great Lakes. Read more
